en: Now, therefore, for the sake of the supreme good of man, there is the inquiry into dharma.
And having known [the Dharma], one who practices it is a righteous person.
He becomes most highly praised in the world after passing away.
And he attains the heavenly world.
Dharma is that which is prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti.
In the absence of that, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭas) is the authority.
Furthermore, the cultured person is one whose self is free from desire.
A phenomenon whose cause is not perceived.
Va.1.8 The region of the Āryas lies to the east of the Ādarśa mountain, to the west of the Kālakavana forest, to the north of the Pāriyātra mountains, and to the south of the Himavat.
And to the north of the Vindhya mountains.
Whatever dharmas and whatever customs exist in that region, all of them are to be accepted everywhere.
But others [are not] for those whose dharma is that of the inverse order.
Some [say] it is even between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
Others say that as far as a black antelope roams, so far extends the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmarcas*).
Furthermore, the Bhāllavins cite this verse in their Nidāna:
To the west is the damming of the Indus, and to the east is the rising of the sun;
as far as the dark one (Kṛṣṇa) runs,
so far indeed extends the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa).

"Whatever those who are advanced in the three Vedas and knowers of dharma may declare here as dharma, whether it be purifying or even more purifying—that is indeed dharma; there is no doubt about this. Thus [it is said].
Manu declared that, due to the absence of Vedic revelation, there are local customs, caste customs, and family customs.
Va.1.18 One who is overtaken by the rising sun (sūryābhyudita) and one who is overtaken by the setting sun (sūryābhinimrukta).
Va.1.19 They declare these to be the five great sins (pañca mahāpātakāni).
Violating the teacher's bed, drinking liquor, causing an abortion, stealing the gold of a Brahmin, and associating with those who have fallen [from their caste]—these are [the great sins].
Either through the Brahmanical bond or through the bond of marriage.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"One falls [from his status] by associating with one who has fallen for the duration of a year."
"One who associates [with such a person] through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage—but not through traveling, sitting together, or giving gifts. (Va. 1.22)
He who casts away the sacred fires,
he who shows hostility toward his teacher,
an atheist, one who lives as an atheist, and one who sells Soma.
Thus end the minor offenses (upapātakas).
A Brāhmaṇa may have three wives in the order of the castes; a Rājanya, two; and a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, one each.
Va.1.25 Some [teachers] say that even a Śūdra woman may be approached in the same manner, with the exception of the recitation of mantras.
One should not act in that manner.
For from this follows the certain ruin of one's family and the loss of heaven after death.
Va.1.28 There are six forms of marriage.
The Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, Kṣātra, and Mānuṣa [forms of marriage].
If one should give a girl who has been previously requested with water, that is the *brāhma* [form of marriage].
When the sacrificial ritual has been spread out and the officiating priest is performing his duty,
one should give a maiden [in marriage].
That which is adorned they call "fate."
And the Ārṣa [form of marriage] is characterized by a pair of cattle.
If he approaches a willing woman of similar birth, that is the Gāndharva marriage.
That which one seizes by force, having violently overpowered [the victim],
is the *kṣātra* (the kṣatriya’s portion).
That which has been purchased with wealth by means of a bargain is "human" (sa mānuṣaḥ).
Therefore, it is understood here that the purchase [of Soma] consists in giving one hundred [cows] plus an extra chariot to one who has a daughter.
"She who, having been purchased by her husband, then behaves [unfaithfully] with others"—
thus it is stated in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Moreover, they cite this:
"Learning that has been lost may return;
but upon the destruction of the family, there is total ruin in this world."
"Even a horse is honored on account of its lineage; therefore, they marry women of noble birth. (Va. 1.38) (c) Thus it is said.
The other three castes should conduct themselves according to the instruction of the Brāhmaṇa.
A Brahmin shall proclaim the duties.
And the king should issue his commands.
But a king, ruling according to dharma, shall take a sixth part of the wealth [as tax].
Except for a Brahmin.
"But he partakes of a sixth share of his sacrifices and charitable works," so it is said.
The Brahmin makes the Veda prosperous;
the Brahmin delivers one from calamities;
therefore, the Brahmin is inviolable.
"Soma becomes his king," so it is said.
"And after death,
there is prosperity"— thus it is known; thus it is known.
Va.2.1 There are four castes: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Va.2.2: The three castes—the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—are the twice-born.
For them,
the first birth is from the mother, and the second is at the binding of the girdle of muñja grass;
herein his mother is said to be Sāvitrī, and his father is called the Ācārya.
Because he bestows the Veda, they call the teacher "father."
Nevertheless, they cite this:

"There are indeed two kinds of seed for a Brahmin man: that which is above the navel and that which is below it. That which is above the navel—by means of that he procreates when he initiates Brahmins."
Whatever he teaches, whatever he sacrifices for others, and whatever good deed he performs—
Now, that which is below the navel— by means of it his own offspring is born here in this world;
therefore they do not say of a learned man who has studied the Vedas, "You are childless."
Hārīta also cites:
"Indeed, no ritual act whatsoever exists for this [person] prior to the binding of the girdle of muñja grass."
"For as long as he is not born into the Veda, he is equal to a Śūdra by virtue of his mode of life. (VaDh 2.6c)
Except for water-libations, *svadhā* offerings, and rites connected with the ancestors.
Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying: "Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak of me to one who is censorious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who is lacking in self-restraint."
And likewise may I be possessed of vigor.
To whomever you know to be pure, vigilant, intelligent, and endowed with celibacy— to him,
who would never deceive you in any way whatsoever,
on that very day you should speak of me.
O Brahman, for the guardian of the treasure.
He who pierces the ears with that which is not false, causing no pain and bestowing immortality.
One should regard him as both father and mother; one should not bear malice toward him on any account whatsoever.
Those Brahmins who, having been taught by their teacher, do not honor him in speech, thought, or deed—
just as they themselves are not to be fed by their teacher.
In that very same way, he does not enjoy that learning.
Just as fire burns dry grass, so does the Brahman that has been questioned with disrespect [burn the questioner].
One should not proclaim the Veda to one who does not show honor, thinking, "It is possible [for me to teach]."
Va.2.13 There are six duties for a Brāhmaṇa.
Va.2.14 Reciting one's own Veda, teaching it, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.
Va.2.15 There are three for a Kṣatriya.
Study, sacrifice, and giving are [the duties].
And the protection of subjects by means of the sword is his own duty; he should live by that.
These same [rites] belong to the Vaiśya.
Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and money-lending.
Service to them is the constant duty of a Śūdra, and that is his prescribed means of livelihood.
Va.2.21 All [the ascetics] must have their hair and dress regulated, or they may all have their hair loose, with the exception of the top-knot.
If they do not live by their own dharma, they should adopt the next lower mode of life.
But one should never [approach] a woman who is superior [in age].
Adopting the livelihood of a Vaiśya, one who lives by trade [must avoid] stones, salt, gems, whetstones, silk, linen, and skins.
And all woven cloth that is dyed red.
Va.2.26 Prepared food, flowers, fruits, roots, fragrances, tastes, water, the juice of medicinal herbs, soma, weapons, poison, meat, milk and its derivatives, iron, tin, lac, and lead.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"One falls immediately from one's caste by [selling] meat, lac, and salt."
"By selling milk, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra in three days. (Va. 2.27)
Among the domestic animals, those with solid hooves and the long-haired ones; all wild animals, birds, and fanged creatures [are not to be eaten].
Regarding grains, they say that sesame seeds are the foremost.
Moreover, they cite this:
"If one performs any act with sesame seeds other than eating, anointing, or giving them away,
having become a worm, he sinks into the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors."
Or alternatively, having themselves plowed and produced sesame seeds, they may sell them.
Therefore, from the time he has testicles until they are bound with a cord before his morning meal, he should be a ploughman.
In the summer, one should offer water.
Va.2.34 "The plough with its iron share, most auspicious, the Soma-pressing [implement], that he sows:
cattle, sheep, and a fat, prolific mare; a wagon and a chariot-yoke."

The plough is sharp-edged, possessed of heroes, accompanied by brave men, and drawn by oxen; it is very auspicious, with a beautiful nose—for its nose is indeed excellent—and by means of that nose it scatters [the seed] and casts [the weeds] far away;
it is "soma-seeking," for Soma reaches him.
He sows that [seed]: cattle, goats, sheep, horses, mules, and camels; and a woman who is fertile, plump, beautiful, auspicious, and a young maiden for the first time.
For how indeed could one sow with a plow?
Except for the sale of grain.
The essences (rasas) are to be analyzed according to their relative superiority or inferiority compared to the Great Principle (mahat).
But one should certainly not [use] salt with savory juices.
One should know that sesame, rice, and cooked food are prescribed for human beings by means of exchange.
According to the *Parivartaka*, a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya who is a usurer shall not pay [the tax].
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"He who, having set aside grain of low value, bestows grain of great value."
Indeed, he is known as a usurer, and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
He weighed the killing of a Brahmin against usury on a scale; the killer of an embryo remained steady at one end, while the usurer trembled at the other.
Or rather, they may at their pleasure give it to one who is more wicked and whose duties have been neglected.
Gold is [to be paid] double, and grain triple.
By means of grain, the [stealing of] liquids is explained.
And flowers, roots, and fruits [are not to be accepted].
That which is weighed on a balance is eightfold [the value of the standard].
Furthermore, they cite this:
"One may take interest for a month of two, three, four, five, or a hundred [percent], as prescribed by tradition."
Of the letters in their successive order.
But by the death of the king, one should destroy the increase of wealth;
yet through the re-consecration of the king, the root of wealth increases once again.
Listen to the interest proclaimed by the words of Vasiṣṭha regarding usury:
"Five māṣas on twenty [kārṣāpaṇas]; thus the dharma is not violated. Va.2.50.
"He does not fall away" (from the root *hā-).
Those who are not learned in the Vedas, who do not recite the sacred formulas, or who do not maintain the sacred fires, become equal in status to Śūdras.
And regarding this, they cite a verse of Manu:
"That twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in another [pursuit],"
Even while still alive, he and his lineage quickly descend to the status of a Śūdra.
He does not become a reciter of the Ṛgveda or a Brāhmaṇa-priest,
nor a merchant, nor an actor;
he does not perform service for a Śūdra.
Neither a thief nor a physician.
That village where twice-born men live as beggars, being devoid of vows and unlearned in the Vedas,
the king should punish;
for it is a provider of sustenance for thieves.
For those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist merely by their birth,
even if they have assembled by the thousands, the status of an assembly does not exist.
Whatever those fools, deluded by darkness and ignorant of the Dharma, say—
that sin becomes a hundredfold.
It reaches those who speak it.
Whether four or even three who have mastered the Vedas should declare something,
that is to be known as Dharma.
Nor [is there any] for others by the thousands.

Sacrificial offerings to the gods (*havya*) and offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*) must always be given to one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*); for what is given to one who is not learned in the Vedas reaches neither the ancestors nor the deities.
If one person in a single household is foolish, even if another is deeply learned— whether he be far away or nearby— one should give to the deeply learned; there is no [gift] for the foolish one.
In the case of a fool, there is transgression.
There is no transgression against a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the Veda;
it is like casting away a blazing fire.
For indeed, no oblation is poured into ashes.
An elephant made of wood, a deer made of leather,
and a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas— these three are merely bearers of names.
Those kingdoms in which the ignorant eat foods fit for the wise meet with drought, or a great calamity arises.
"Fear," it is said.
If one who is not known [to be a Brahmin] should acquire [the status], provided he is engaged in the six duties of a Brahmin.
The king shall not take it.
Having killed an assassin who is currently attacking,
they say that there is no sin whatsoever for the one who takes his life.
Moreover, they cite this:
"The incendiary, the poisoner, the one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and likewise the one who seizes land or a wife— these six are *ātatāyins* (assassins)."
Even if he is one who has mastered the end of the Vedas,
one may strike back against an assassin who approaches with intent to kill;
by doing so, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin.
He who kills an assailant who has come with intent to harm— even if that assailant is born of a family devoted to Vedic study—
does not thereby become a slayer of an embryo.
"Anger encounters that anger. (c) Thus it is said.

One who has performed the *triṇāciketa* sacrifice five times; one who maintains the five sacred fires; one who knows the *tri-suparṇa*; one who has performed the four *medha* sacrifices; a follower of the *Vājasaneyin* school; one who knows the six Vedāṅgas; one whose lineage has been sustained by the giving of Brahman-knowledge; a singer of the *Chandoga* hymns; one who chants the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*; one who knows both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas;
and one whose maternal and paternal lineages for ten generations are known to have been learned in the Veda (*śrotriya*). These are those from whom one studies the Dharmas.
These learned men who have completed their vows (snātakas) become purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvanas).
One who is versed in the four Vedas, one who is capable of critical analysis, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), and a reciter of the Dharma—
these three types of persons established in their respective stages of life (*āśrama*) constitute an assembly (*parṣad*), provided they number at least ten.
Having initiated him, he should teach him the entire Veda; such a person is an *ācārya*.
But he who teaches a single portion [of the Veda] is an *upādhyāya*.
And he who knows the Vedāṅgas.
Va.3.24 For the protection of themselves and for the defense of the social orders, the Brāhmaṇa and the Vaiśya may take up arms.
But for a Kṣatriya, that [study] is indeed obligatory, because he has the duty to protect [the people].

Having washed both feet and the hands up to the wrists, sitting facing either east or north, one should sip water three times with the *brāhma-tīrtha*— the line above the root of the thumb— without making a sound.
He should wipe it twice.
Va.3.28 One should touch the cavities with water.
One should pour water over the head and into the left hand.
Walking,
standing, or lying down.
Or, if one is prostrate, one should not sip water for purification.
A Brāhmaṇa [should sip water] with water that reaches the heart, which is free from bubbles and free from froth.
But with those reaching the throat, a Kṣatriya.
A Vaiśya [is purified] by water that has been sipped.
And likewise, [one becomes impure] by touching a woman or a Śūdra who have been touched [by an impure person].
Even from a small opening, those cows which are capable of passing through a leaf are [to be considered as having passed].
{BṣPṣ taparṇa}{F tarpaṇa} Va.3.36: Nor [should one offer] those things which are corrupted by color, smell, or taste, nor those that bring inauspicious results.
Va.3.37 Drops that do not fall from the mouth and are not touched by the limbs do not make one impure through leavings.
Having slept, having eaten, having sneezed.
having drunk, having wept, having bathed.
And having sipped water again,
he should put on his garment.
Va.3.39 Where the two lips touch one another and are hairless.
Va.3.40 There is no offense regarding the residue remaining on the beard.
Va.3.41 Just as with the teeth, so it is with food particles stuck between them; whatever may be inside the mouth, one becomes pure simply by swallowing it.
Even when one causes others to sip water,
those drops that fall upon the feet do not cause one to become ritually impure by means of them.
These, however, are traditionally taught as being comprised within the stages (bhūmi).
Va.3.43 If, while walking or during meals, he should happen to touch something that is leavings,
he should set that object down on the ground, sip water, and then [resume].
One should practice again.
Whatever may be worthy of investigation,
one should touch it with water.
Wild animals killed by dogs, fruit fallen by birds, that which has been trodden upon by children, and that which has been frequented by women; [these are forbidden].
And whatever merchandise has been displayed, as well as those faults found in the faces of women.
He is not harmed by mosquitoes or flies that have settled upon him. Having carefully examined the waters on the ground that satisfy the cows, [he should use them].
Prajāpati declared all of them to be impure.
Va.3.48: Purification for that which is smeared with impurity consists in removing the stain and odor by means of water and earth.
Va.3.49 For objects made of metal, clay, wood, and woven fibers, the methods of purification are respectively: ash, wiping, burning, and washing.
Va.3.50 The same [rule] applies to crystals and gems as it does to fire.
The [impurity] of pearls, conch-shells, and mother-of-pearl is like that of gems.
Va.3.52 The rules regarding bones are like those regarding wood.
Va.3.53: The purification of ropes, split bamboo, and leather is like that of cloth.
Va.3.54 [The measurement] of vessels made of fruit is by means of cow-hair [strands].
Va.3.55 For those made of linen, [the purification is] with a paste of white mustard seeds.

But for the ground, purification is attained according to the specific nature of the defect by means of sweeping, scraping with a stone, sprinkling, and smearing with cow-dung, each applied to its proper place.
{BṣPṣ upalena}{E upalepana} Va.3.57 Moreover, they also cite:
Va.3.57 By digging, by burning, by trampling, and even by treading over with cows.
The ground is purified by four things, and by the fifth, by smearing it with cow-dung.
A woman is purified by her menses; a river is purified by its current;
[a vessel] is purified by ashes.
Furthermore, bell-metal [is purified] by repeated heating, and earthenware [is purified] by firing.
An earthen vessel that has been touched by intoxicating liquors, urine, or feces, or by phlegm, pus, tears, or blood,
is not purified even by re-firing.
"Limbs are purified by water;
the mind is purified by truth;
the elemental self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom. Thus it is said.
Gold is purified by water alone.
Likewise, silver [is not perceived].
Copper is purified by an acid.
At the base of the little finger is the divine *tīrtha*.
Va.3.65: For the sages, [the measure] is one finger-breadth.
On the tips of the fingers, it is human.
The center of the palm is sacred to Agni.
The space between the forefinger and the thumb is for the ancestors.
Thinking, "It pleases me," one should praise the evening and morning meals.
"May it be well-savored," [one says] at a rite for the ancestors.
Va.3.71: "It is accomplished" (*saṃpannam*) [is used] in the case of each and every auspicious rite (*ābhyudayika*). Va.4.1:
Furthermore, the fourfold caste system is distinguished by its original nature and by specific purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth;
the Rājanya was made from his arms;
that which was the Vaiśya was his thighs; from his feet the Śūdra was born.
There is also a Vedic citation (nigama) stating: "The two thighs are the Śūdra" (ŚB 4.2).

With the *gāyatrī* he created the Brāhmaṇa, with the *triṣṭubh* the Rājanya, and with the *jagatī* the Vaiśya; but with no *chandas* at all did he create the Śūdra—thus it is known that he is not to undergo the sacraments (*asaṃskārya*).
For all [these], truthfulness, freedom from anger, generosity, non-violence, and procreation are essential.
"One should not harm even an animal for the sake of honoring ancestors, deities, or guests"—
this is the teaching of Manu.
"In the honey-mixture offering, in a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors and the gods—
it is only on these occasions that one may kill an animal,
and not otherwise; so Manu has declared."

Meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings; nor does the slaughter of living beings lead to heaven. Therefore, in a sacrifice, what is called "killing" is actually no killing at all.
Furthermore, they cook a large bull or a large goat for a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya who has arrived as a guest;
in this way, they provide hospitality to him.
And the purification consisting of water-libations begins from the second year [of age].
According to some, [the period lasts] until the eruption of teeth.
Having consigned the body to the fire, they descend into the water without looking back.
They should perform the water-rites with both hands, using the left hand for the other [hand], facing south on days with an odd number.
With both hands, [one should offer]; for this southern direction indeed belongs to the ancestors.
Having gone to their houses, they should remain for three days on a layer of grass without eating.
If they are unable [to subsist by their own means], they should live on what has been purchased or produced.
A ten-day period of impurity due to death is prescribed for the sapinda relatives.
Sapiṇḍa-relationship is understood to extend up to the seventh person.
And for women who have been given away in marriage, it is understood that the impurity lasts for three generations.
The others shall perform [the funeral rites] for those who have been given away in marriage, and they [in turn] shall perform them for those [others].
The same would apply even in the case of birth for those who desire purity that is not merely superficial.
Or [the name] of the mother and father. Va.4.21.
Some say it is because the mother is the cause of that [birth].
Moreover, they also cite this:

"There is no impurity for a man during childbirth (*sūtaka*) if he does not come into contact [with it]. In that case, it is the *rajas* (menstrual blood) that should be known as impure, and that is not found in a man."
If that period should end and another period should again occur, they shall be purified by the remainder of the first period.
Va.4.25: When a night remains, [one should recite] with two [verses].
At dawn, with three [verses].
A Brahmin [is purified] in ten nights.
A Kṣatriya [should perform] the fifteen-night sacrifice.
A Vaiśya [becomes purified] after twenty nights.
A Śūdra is purified in one month.
Moreover, they cite this:
"He who eats during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, or even during a birth-impurity,
shall go [to hell]."
He is born in the terrible hells and in the womb of animals.

Va.4.32: A twice-born man who, having been invited, eats at a funeral feast held within ten days of the death or when the corpse is still present, becomes a worm at the end of his body and consumes that very excrement. Thus it is said.
By studying the Saṃhitā while fasting for twelve months or twelve half-months,
one becomes purified.
Thus it is known.
Va.4.34 When a child dies before reaching two years of age, or in the case of a miscarriage, the period of impurity for the sapinda relatives is three nights.
Gautama says that there is immediate purification.
If one hears that a person residing in another region has died after the ten-day period has passed, the period of impurity lasts for one night.
If one who has maintained the sacred fires should die while traveling abroad, having performed the rite of re-consecration (punar-saṃskāra), [he should be cremated].
"Purity is like that of a corpse," says Gautama.

Having touched a sacrificial post, a funeral pyre, a cremation ground, a menstruating woman, a woman who has recently given birth, or anything impure, one should enter the water with the head uncovered, saying "Water! Water! (apaḥ).
A woman is not independent; she has man as her primary authority.
It is known from tradition that those who do not maintain the sacred fires or who are menstruating may be addressed as "immortal" (amṛta).
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth."
And a son, when he has reached old age, [should support his mother]; a woman does not deserve independence. (c) Thus.
Va.5.4: Regarding her, the expiation for the husband's malevolent incantation has been declared in the secret [sections].
For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
A woman in her menses remains impure for three nights.
She should not apply collyrium,
nor should she anoint herself with oil, nor should she bathe in water.
One should sleep on the ground,
not sleep during the day,
and one should not touch fire.
One should not spin thread, nor should one brush one's teeth,
nor should one eat meat.
One should not gaze at the planets, one should not laugh,
and one should not perform any such action.
One should not drink from a small vessel, nor should one drink with cupped hands, nor with a vessel made of red metal.
Or rather, it is known from scripture: "Indra, having slain the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ... Va.5.8. Indeed, this is understood.
Thinking of himself thus, "I am seized by evil and bound by great unrighteousness," all beings reviled him, crying out, "Bhrūṇahan! Bhrūṇahan! (O slayer of the embryo!)
He ran to the women, saying, "Accept a third part of this guilt of killing an embryo for me.
They said,
"What would accrue to us?"
He said,
"Choose a boon.
They replied:

"May we obtain offspring in season," they said; "may we unite until the time of childbirth," they added. "So be it," they replied, and they accepted [the union]. This very act of destroying the embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*) manifests month after month.
Therefore, one should not eat the food of a woman in her menses;
she remains there having assumed the very form of the murder of an embryo.
Regarding this, they say: "Cosmetic ointment and oil for anointing are not to be accepted from her, for that is the food of women.
Therefore, people feel disgust toward her and toward those things.
"May she not come near me."
"Those among whom women remain menstruating, those who are without sacred fires,
and those whose family lacks Vedic learning— all these follow the dharma of Śūdras."
All of them follow the dharma of Śūdras.
It is certain that for all people, conduct is the supreme dharma;
one whose soul is overwhelmed by deficient conduct perishes both in this world and after death.
Neither austerities, nor sacred knowledge, nor the Agnihotra sacrifice,
nor sacrificial fees can ever rescue one who has fallen away from this [path] due to deficient conduct.
The Vedas, even if studied together with the six auxiliary sciences, do not purify one who is deficient in conduct;
the sacred hymns abandon such a person at the time of death.
Like birds that have grown wings leaving their nest.
But for a Brahmin who is deficient in conduct, even the Vedas with their six auxiliary limbs and all the sacrifices are incapable of producing any joy,
just as beautiful wives are to a blind man.
The Vedic meters do not deliver him from evil who is deceitful and lives by deceit;
even though both syllables are being studied correctly.
That Brahman purifies [the one who recites it], just as the rains purify the crops.
For a man of evil conduct in this world becomes censured;
he is constantly a partaker of suffering, afflicted by disease, and short-lived indeed.
From right conduct, dharma bears fruit; from right conduct, wealth bears fruit;
through right conduct, one attains prosperity.
And [it is] the absence of the characteristic of conduct.
Even a man who is devoid of all auspicious marks, if he is of virtuous conduct,
full of faith, and free from envy, lives for a hundred years.
One who knows the Dharma should ensure that his activities regarding food, excretion, and recreation are well-restrained;
likewise, his speech, mental actions, ascetic penance, as well as his wealth and lifespan, must be kept most carefully guarded.
Va.6.10 One should void both urine and feces facing north during the day; at night, however, one should do so facing south.
In this way, indeed, one's life-span is not harmed.
Facing the fire, facing the sun, facing a cow, and facing a Brahmin;
facing Soma, water, and the twilight—[if one urinates] in these directions, one's wisdom perishes.
One should not urinate in a river,
nor on a path, nor in ashes;
nor in cow dung, nor in a ploughed field, nor in a sown field, nor in the shade of trees that provide livelihood for grass-eaters.
In shadow or in darkness, by night or by day, O twice-born one,
one may face whichever direction is comfortable,
as well as when there is fear of danger to life.
One should perform the ritual actions with water that has been drawn out [of the vessel].
Va.6.15 One may bathe even with water that has not been drawn up [from a well or river].
A Brahmin should fetch clay from a riverbank that contains sand.

The five types of earth remaining after purification— namely, that from within water, from a temple, from an anthill, from a mouse-hole, or from a place where earth was previously used for purification— should not be taken.
One application of clay is prescribed for the penis, three for each hand— thus two applications of clay are traditionally taught—
and five for the anus, ten for one foot, and seven for both feet.
This purification prescribed for householders is twofold for students,
threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
A sage’s meal consists of eight morsels, that of a forest-dweller sixteen,
that of a householder thirty-two, and for a student there is no fixed limit.
The man who maintains the sacred fires, the ox, and the student— these three succeed even while they are not eating.
Nor is there success for those who do not eat.
In the observances and restraints, and in the duties of sacrifice and study.
Yoga, austerity, self-control, charity, truthfulness, purity, sacred learning, compassion, knowledge, realization, and faith— this is the characteristic of a Brahmin.
One should recognize long-standing enmity, envy, untruthfulness, reviling of Brahmins, slander,
and mercilessness as the characteristics of a Śūdra.

Those Brahmins who are peaceful and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with sacred learning, who have conquered their senses, who have desisted from killing living beings, and who hold back their outstretched hands from accepting gifts— they alone are capable of delivering others across [the ocean of existence].
One vessel consists of the Veda, and another vessel consists of austerity;
yet among all vessels, that one is the true vessel whose stomach contains no food from a Śūdra.
If a twice-born man dies while the food of a Śūdra remains in his stomach,
he shall become a village pig or be born into that Śūdra’s family.
One whose limbs are nourished by the food and essence of a Śūdra, even if he studies constantly, or performs fire-sacrifices, or mutters prayers,
does not attain the higher goal.
But he who engages in sexual intercourse after having eaten the food of a Śūdra—
his sons belong to the one whose food it was, and he himself shall not ascend to heaven.
One who has risen through Vedic study, who possesses a noble birth, who is tranquil, established in the maintenance of the sacred fires, who fears sin, who is highly learned,
who is patient toward women, who is righteous, a refuge for cows, and exhausted by religious observances— such a person they call a worthy recipient.
Just as milk, curd, ghee, or honey placed in an unbaked clay vessel would perish due to the weakness of the vessel—
neither the vessel nor those liquids would remain— so it is with the mind.
In this way, an ignorant man who accepts cows, gold, clothing, a horse, land,
or sesame seeds is reduced to ashes.
(c) Like a piece of wood.
One should not practice scratching with the fingernails.
And one should not eat food with the fingernails at the beginning of a meal.
And one should not drink water with cupped hands.
One should not strike the water with one's foot or hand.
One should not [wash] water with water.
One should not strike a fruit with bricks.
One fruit does not [arise] from another fruit.
One should not be a schemer nor a deceiver.
One should not learn the language of the Mlecchas.
Moreover, they cite this:
"One should not be fickle with hands and feet, nor fickle with the eyes;
nor should one be fickle with speech or limbs—this is the sphere of the disciplined."
Those Brāhmaṇas whose Veda, along with its supplements, has been transmitted through an unbroken lineage, and who have direct perception of the Śruti, are to be known as the learned (śiṣṭas).
He whom no one knows— whether as existing or non-existing, as unlearned or widely learned, as well-behaved or ill-behaved— that man is a Brāhmaṇa.
"He is a brahmin," [he said].
Va.7.1 There are four stages of life (āśramas).
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the wandering mendicant.
Having studied one Veda,
two Vedas, or all the Vedas among them, and having remained firm in his vow of studentship (*brahmacarya*), he may dwell with whomever he desires.
A religious student (brahmacārī) shall attend upon his teacher until the liberation from the body [i.e., death].
And when the teacher has died, one should tend the sacred fire.
For it is known that Agni is your teacher.
Restrained in speech.
One who eats at the fourth, sixth, and eighth meal-times.
He should practice begging for alms.
He is dependent upon his teacher.
He may have matted hair, or his hair may be matted only at the topknot.
When the teacher is walking, one should follow him;
when he is seated, one should sit.
Whether standing,
lying down, or sitting.
One should attend upon.
One who studies when summoned.
Having offered everything that has been obtained, he should eat it with their permission.
He shall avoid using a bedstead, lying down, brushing his teeth, washing himself, applying collyrium, anointing with oil, sandals, and an umbrella.
He should stand during the day and sit during the night.
Three times a day he should approach the water, saying "Apsas! Apsas! three times.

Va.8.1 A householder, having subdued anger and joy and being permitted by his teacher, shall bathe and take a wife who is not descended from the same *ṛṣi* lineage, who has not had sexual intercourse with another, who is younger than himself, and who is of equal status.
Va.8.2 [She should be] fifth in descent from his mother’s relatives and seventh from his father’s relatives.
He should kindle the nuptial fire.
One should not turn away a guest who has arrived in the evening.
One should not dwell in his house without eating.
If a Brahmin seeking clothing comes to someone's house and does not eat,
whatever merit that person has earned, he takes it all away.
He goes (gam-).
A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is considered a guest (*atithi*);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore called a guest.

A Brahmin who is a resident of the same village, as well as one who is merely a casual acquaintance, is not considered a guest; whether food is available at the proper time or not, one must not let such a person go hungry.
He may dwell in a house.
One who possesses faith and virtue and is free from covetousness is fully capable of establishing the sacred fires; he should not remain one who has not established the fires.
And one who does not sacrifice with Soma is not fit for the Soma [sacrifice].
He should be devoted to Vedic study, sacrifice, and procreation.
One should honor a guest who has arrived at one's house by rising from one's seat, offering a seat, speaking kind words, and being free from envy.
And one should sustain all beings with food according to one's ability.
The householder alone performs sacrifice;
the householder practices austerity. Of the four stages of life, the householder is indeed preeminent.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
even so do all those in the various stages of life find their support in the householder.
(And) its persistence.
Just as all living beings live by depending upon their mother,
even so do [all others] depend upon the householder.
All the mendicants live.
He should always carry water with him, always wear the sacrificial thread, always engage in the private recitation of the Veda, and avoid the food of outcasts;
he should approach his wife during her season and offer oblations according to the prescribed rules.
A Brahmin does not fall from the world of Brahmā.
"From the world of Brahmā," thus [it is said].
Va.9.1 A forest-dweller (vānaprastha) has matted hair and wears garments of bark or deerskin.
And he should not enter a village.
Va.9.3 One should not stand upon ground that has been ploughed with a plough.
He should gather roots and fruits that have grown wild.
Va.9.5 One who is a perpetual celibate.
One whose intention is directed toward the higher realms.
One should honor a guest who has arrived at the hermitage with alms consisting of roots and fruits.
One should indeed give, but one should not accept.
He should touch water for purification three times a day.
Having kindled the fire according to the ascetic rite,
one becomes a maintainer of the sacred fires (āhitāgni).
Va.9.11 One who has the root of a tree as his dwelling, after six months, shall be without fire and without a fixed abode.
He who gives to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings shall go to the infinite heaven; thus it is called "the infinite."
The wandering mendicant, having given the gift of fearlessness to all beings, should depart.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The sage who wanders about after having granted fearlessness to all beings..."
For him as well, there shall never be any fear from any living beings whatsoever.
But he who, having granted safety to all beings, turns back from it; (Va.10.3)
Having accepted material goods, he destroys both those beings who have been born and those yet unborn.
One may renounce all ritual actions, but one must not renounce the Veda.
By renouncing the Veda, one becomes a Śūdra; therefore, one must not renounce the Veda.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath-restraint is the supreme austerity. Begging is superior to fasting, and compassion excels giving. Thus it is said.
Shaven-headed, without a sense of "mine," and without possessions.
One should go for alms to seven houses that have not been previously designated.
When the smoke has subsided and the pestle has been set aside.
Va.10.9 Wearing a single garment.
Or, having covered his body with a deerskin or with grass cut from a cow-pen.
Va.10.11 He is one who sleeps on the bare ground.
One should dwell in an impermanent residence.
At the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the foot of a tree.
One who studies knowledge with the mind.
He is one who constantly dwells in the forest.
One should not walk about while looking at domestic animals.

For one who is constantly dwelling in the forest, whose senses are conquered, who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses, whose mind is intent on contemplation of the inner self, and who remains equanimous—there is indeed certain non-returning. Thus it is said.
One whose outward signs are unmanifest and whose conduct is unmanifest.
One who is not insane but wears the garb of one who is insane.
Moreover, they cite this:
"Liberation is not for one who delights in the science of grammar, nor for one who delights in winning over the world."
Not for one intent on food and clothing, nor even for one fond of pleasant dwellings.
Nor should he ever seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks,
nor by instructions or discourses.
In the absence of gain, one should not be despondent;
nor indeed should one rejoice upon obtaining it. One should possess only what is necessary for the maintenance of life.
Free from attachment to sense-objects.
"He who has no attachment to a hut, nor to water, nor to clothing, nor to the triple-tufted hair;
who has no attachment to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food—he indeed is a knower of liberation."
In a brahmin family, he may eat as much as he obtains,
both morning and evening, with the exception of honey and meat.
And one should not be satisfied.
Or he may dwell in a village.
He is not crooked,
not deceitful, not seeking refuge [in the wrong], and not fickle.
And one should not engage in sensory contact with anyone at all.
He is indifferent toward all beings by avoiding both injury and favor.

The avoidance of backbiting, envy, arrogance, egoism, lack of faith, dishonesty, self-praise, disparagement of others, hypocrisy, greed, delusion, anger, and malice is the dharma desired for all stages of life.

A Brāhmaṇa who wears the sacrificial thread, holds a water-pot in his hand, remains pure, and avoids the food of a Śūdra, does not fall from the world of Brahman— from the world of Brahman— so it is said.
There are six who are worthy of the guest-offering (argha).
The officiating priest, the bridegroom, the king, the paternal uncle, the graduate, and the maternal uncle [are to be honored].
Having prepared the Vaiśvadeva food, one should offer oblations in the domestic fire every morning and evening.
One should offer an oblation to the household deities.
Having given the first portion to a learned Vedic scholar or to a student of sacred knowledge, he should immediately thereafter offer it to the ancestors.
Then he should feed the guest, honoring each more distinguished one in successive order.
Among those belonging to one's own household, [there are] girls, children, the elderly, the young, and women who have recently given birth.
Then he should take other domestic [fires].
One should scatter [the food] on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, outcasts, and crows.
One may give to a Śūdra either the remains of one's meal or that which is not the remains.
The husband and wife should eat the remainder.

Va.11.12 If a guest should arrive when the Vaiśvadeva offering has already been set aside, one should have special food prepared for him using all available resources, even if it requires cooking again.
For it is known:
"The Vaiśvānara enters the house as a Brāhmaṇa guest; therefore, they bring water for him."
For people know that peace to come from rain is indeed [the result of] food.
Having fed him, one should attend upon him.
One should follow him as far as the boundary, or until one receives permission to depart.
In the dark fortnight, after the fourth day, one should give to the ancestors.

On the previous day, having assembled the Brahmins— whether they be ascetics, householders, or virtuous men— who are not yet advanced in age, who do not engage in improper occupations, who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), and who are neither formal students (*śiṣya*) nor resident pupils (*antevāsin*).
One should also feed disciples who possess virtuous qualities.
Excluding those who are naked, white-skinned, eunuchs, blind, those with black teeth, lepers, and those with deformed nails.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Furthermore, if one who knows the mantras is disciplined, even if he is afflicted by bodily defects that defile the company,
Yama has declared him to be irreproachable."
He indeed is one who purifies the assembly.
At a *śrāddha*, the remnants of the food must not be removed until the end of the day;
for streams of nectar flow from them, and those [ancestors] drink them.
Those for whom the water-libation has not been performed.
One should not wipe away the remnants until the sun has set;
for from there, streams of milk flow forth.
They are inexhaustible and share in the movement [of the world].
It is the established rule that for those of one's own lineage who have died before the performance of the purificatory rites,
Manu has declared both the food left on the dish and the remnants of the meal to be their allotted portion.
One should offer the food remnants on the ground, the scattered grains, and the water used for washing as food for those deceased who are childless and short-lived.
When food has been offered to the ancestors with both hands released,
the evil-minded Asuras indeed watch for that interval.
Therefore, one should not perform the welcoming of food or partake of a meal with empty hands.
One should remain standing while both [the teacher and the pupil] are eating the remnants.
Two [should be invited] for the rite for the gods, three for the ancestral rite, or one for each of the two.
Even if one is very wealthy, one should feed [the monks] but should not become attached to a large assembly.
Hospitality, proper place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmin—
these five things are destroyed by prolixity;
therefore, one should avoid it.
Or else, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, and who is free from all inauspicious marks.
Va.11.30 If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how can there be a portion for the gods?
Having taken food from the vessel, [one should offer it].
But for everything that has been mentioned as the subject matter.
Having established [the image] in a temple of the deity,
one should then perform the śrāddha;
or one should cast it [into the water].
One should either offer that food into the fire or give it to a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*).
As long as the food remains warm and as long as they eat with speech restrained,
for so long do the ancestors eat.
...until the qualities of the sacrificial oblation have been described.
The qualities of the sacrificial oblation (havis) should not be mentioned as long as the ancestors have not been satiated;
once the ancestors have been satiated, they may be mentioned afterwards.
The oblation is excellent.
But an ascetic who, having been appointed to a *śrāddha* or a rite for the gods, should discard meat,
falls into hell for as many years as there are hairs on the animal's body.
At a *śrāddha*, three things are purifying: a daughter’s son, kusha grass, and sesame seeds;
and in this regard, they praise three other qualities:
purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
When the sun becomes dim during the eighth part of the day,
that time should be known as *ku-tapas*.
What is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
He who, having given and having eaten at a funeral feast (śrāddha),
engages in sexual intercourse;
His ancestors become consumers of his semen for that entire month.
The embryo that is born from that [act], after having given and having enjoyed.
And he does not obtain his paternal inheritance; moreover, he is born with a diminished lifespan. (Va. 11.38)
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
wait upon the newborn son just as birds wait upon the fig tree.
"With honey, meat, vegetables, milk, and milk-rice—
this man will offer us the śrāddha during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism."
A son who increases the lineage and is diligent in the duties toward his father.
Those born before rejoice in that which is endowed with gods and brahmins.
The ancestors rejoice at him who, while staying at Gayā, gives gifts, just as farmers do at their well-tilled fields.
"O ancestors, through that [food], you possess sons. (c) Thus.
One should offer to the ancestors on the full moon days of Śrāvaṇa and Āgrahāyaṇī, and also on the Anvaṣṭakā day.
In the case of the two Āgrahāyaṇī festivals,
there is no restriction regarding the time, provided that the ritual materials, the location, and the Brahmins are present.
A Brahmin must certainly establish the sacred fires.
And one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi, Cāturmāsya, Paśu, and Soma sacrifices.
For this is both a fixed obligation and is commended as a debt.
For it is known:

"A Brahmin is born burdened with three debts—by sacrifice to the gods, by progeny to the ancestors, and by the life of a student (brahmacarya) to the seers. He indeed is free from debt who has sacrificed, who has a son, and who has lived as a student.
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception.
In the eighth year from conception for a Brāhmaṇa, and in the eleventh year from conception for a Rājanya.
A Vaiśya [should be initiated] in the twelfth years from conception.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Palāśa wood.
Or, for a Kṣatriya, it may be made of nyagrodha wood.
Or, for a Vaiśya, it may be made of udumbara wood.
The sacrificial cord of a Brāhmaṇa should reach up to his hair.
The [staff] of a kṣatriya is level with the forehead.
Va.11.57 The nose-length is indeed for the Vaiśya.
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa shall be made of muñja grass.
Va.11.59 A bowstring [is the emblem] of a Kṣatriya.
The garment made of hemp fibers belongs to the Vaiśya.
A black antelope skin serves as the upper garment for a Brāhmaṇa.
Va.11.62 For a Kṣatriya, the Raurava [sāman].
For a Vaiśya, it shall be the skin of a cow or a goat.
A white, unwashed garment is for a Brāhmaṇa.
Va.11.65 A kṣatriya’s [should be] madder-red.
For a Vaiśya, it shall be yellow or made of silk.
Or, for all [of these], woven cloth that is not dyed [is permitted].
A Brahmin should ask for alms, placing the word "bhavat" (sir) at the beginning.
A member of the royal caste (rājanya) has *bhavat* as his middle [honorific title].
A Vaiśya [should address] one who ends with "bhavat."
For a Brāhmaṇa, the time [for initiation] does not expire until the sixteenth year.
For a Kṣatriya, up to twenty-two years.
For a Vaiśya, [the period of impurity lasts] up to twenty-four days.
From this point forward, they become those for whom the Sāvitrī has been lost.
One should not initiate them, nor teach them, nor perform sacrifices for them.
They should not marry with these.
One whose *sāvitrī* has fallen shall perform the *uddālaka-vrata*.
For two months he should subsist on barley-gruel;

for one month on milk; for half a month on curdled milk (*āmikṣā*); for eight nights on clarified butter; for six nights on unsolicited food; for three nights he should subsist on water; and for one day and night he should fast.
One should go to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Or he should sacrifice with the Vrātyastoma;
"or he should sacrifice, or he should sacrifice."
Now, therefore, follow the observances for one who has completed his Vedic studies (the Snātaka).
He should not beg from anyone,
except for the attendants of the king.
But one who is overcome by hunger may beg for something— be it a field, whether cultivated or uncultivated, a cow, a goat or sheep, or finally, gold, grain, or food.
But the instruction is that a *snātaka* should not perish from hunger.
One should not live together with one who wears soiled clothes.
Not by one who is menstruating.
Va.12.7 Not with one who is unsuitable.
One who is not a *kulaṃkula* shall not be so.
One should not step over a stretched calf-rope.
One should not look at the sun as it rises, nor as it sets.
One should not void urine or excrement in water.
One should not spit.
Having covered the ground with sacrificially forbidden grass, one whose head is wrapped [with a cloth] should void urine and feces;
facing north during the day and facing south at night, and one should sit toward the north during the two twilights.

Regarding urine and feces: moreover, they cite [the following]: "For *snātakas*, however, this [ablution] should be constant. *Vaśiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra* 12.14. Then they also cite: *Vaśiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra* 12.14: "But for *snātakas*, it should be constant."
Likewise, an inner garment and an upper garment;
two sacrificial threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water.
In water, in the hand, and in wood, it is declared that [the water] is pure even when [the vessel] is in fire;
therefore, one should wipe the water-pot with both hands and water.
For Manu, Prajāpati, has declared this to be the carrying of fire around [the victim].
And having performed the obligatory duties, one should sip water for purification; thus it is said by those who possess the highest knowledge of purity.
One should eat food facing the east.
One should swallow the entire morsel silently, with the thumb included.
And one should not make a sound.
He should approach his own wife during her fertile period, avoiding the forbidden days.
He should not approach [her] from the side.
But he who performs sexual intercourse in the mouth of a married woman becomes [a sinner].
His ancestors consume his semen for that month;
whatever pleasure he derives from unchaste conduct is based on unrighteousness.
Moreover, it is known in the *Kaṭhaka*:
"May our daughters, when they are about to give birth tomorrow, lie down with their husbands."
Thus was the boon granted to women by Indra.
One should not climb a tree.
One should not descend into a well.
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth.
One should not pass between the fire and a Brahmin.
Not [the elision of *a*] after two fires.
Nor [should one eat] from two Brahmins, whether they have given permission or not.
"One should not eat together with one's wife; thus it is known in the Vājasaneyaka that the offspring will lack vigor."
One should not point it out by the name "rainbow" (indradhanus).
One should say, "a jeweled bow."
One should avoid a seat made of *palāśa* wood, sandals, and a tooth-stick made of *palāśa*.
One should not eat from one's lap.
One should not eat while sitting on a low seat.
One should carry a staff made of bamboo.
And [the wearing of] golden neck-ornaments and earrings.
One should not wear a garland outside [the house],
except for one made of gold.
And one should avoid assemblies and gatherings.
Moreover, they cite this:
"The invalidation of the Vedas and the reviling of the Ṛṣis,
as well as a lack of discipline in all matters— this is the destruction of the self."
One who has not been invited should not go to a sacrifice;
if he should go, he must return by way of circumambulation.
One should not set out upon a path until the sun has risen above the trees.
And one should not board a boat that is in a state of uncertainty.
One should not cross a river with one's arms.
Having risen during the latter part of the night and studied, he should not go back to sleep again.
During the *muhūrta* sacred to Prajāpati, a Brāhmaṇa should observe certain restraints; he should indeed observe them.
Now, therefore, follows the commencement of Vedic study (*svādhyāya-upākarma*), on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or of Prauṣṭhapada.
Having kindled the fire, he offers parched grains as oblations.
"To the gods, to the seers, and to the meters."
Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce a blessing and having consumed curd, they should then commence the formal study of the Vedic texts.
For four and a half months, or five and a half months.
From this point forward, one should study during the bright fortnights.
But the Vedāṅgas may be studied at will.
Va.13.8 These are his days when study is forbidden.
Va.13.9 [It is forbidden to study] when there is thunder at twilight.
At the twilights.
In cities where there is a corpse inside or where there is public proclamation during the day.
Alternatively, it may be done on ground that has been smeared with cow-dung or swept clean, as one desires.
At the edge of a cemetery.
[The rule] for one who is lying down. // Va.13.14 // Śaya.āna. // 14 //
Va.13.15 [It is an offense] for one who performs a *śrāddha* ceremony.
And in this regard, they cite this verse of Manu:
"Having accepted fruits, water, sesame seeds, food, and whatever else may be offered at a *śrāddha*," Va.13.16.
"Furthermore, Brāhmaṇas are traditionally remembered as those whose hands are their mouths. (c)
Va.13.17 [The rules apply] to one running,
to a foul odor and the like, and to barren soil.
[The same applies] to one who has climbed a tree. Va.13.18.
And [the same applies] on a boat and in an army.
And having eaten while one's hands are still wet.
Va.13.21 Regarding the sound of an arrow.
On the fourteenth day, on the new moon day, on the eighth day, and on the Aṣṭakā days.
And [the same applies] to one who has extended his legs and rests upon his lap.
Va.13.24 [One should study] in the presence of the teacher.
